newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia car sales seen lower in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia car sales seen lower in 1997.

text.p: Year-on-year sales of passenger cars in Malaysia are estimated to have fallen by nearly half in 1996, and could stabilise or decline further in 1997, industry analysts said.
Sales jumped 44.4 percent in 1995, owing to the launch of new models and a buoyant economy. But analysts said they expected only 24 percent growth this year, and between 15 and 20 percent in 1997.
"The Malaysian car market is still strong but it's tapering off," Loke Chee Kien, an automobile analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Kuala Lumpur, said.
"Last year was a bumper year as it coincided with the peak of the five-year cycle when Malaysians change their cars," he said. "I think next year's growth will be in commercial vehicles."
Loke said a booming construction and manufacturing industry has fuelled demand for trucks and vans in Malaysia.

Sales of assorted commercial vehicles, including four-wheel-drives (4WDs) registered for business, grew 48 percent in the first 10 months of 1996, compared to 20 percent between January and October 1995.
The Malaysian Motor Traders Association said 225,554 cars, including 4WDs for private use, were sold in the first 10 months of this year.

Analysts expect full sales for 1996 to reach 278,000 units. This means a 24 percent rise from the 224,991 cars sold in 1995, but is still lower than the 44.4 percent jump seen between 1994 and 1995, when only 155,765 units were sold.
Economists said the declining year-on-year percentage in car sales was also due to government attempts to curb consumer spending in anticipation of an economic slowdown.
The government has forecast an economic expansion of 8.2 percent in 1996 and 8.0 percent in 1997, against the 9.5 percent achieved in 1995.
Loke said he expected sales in 1997 to grow by 15 percent to around 316,000 units, but some analysts were optimistic of a higher figure.

"I think we'll still have about 20 percent (growth) or more next year," said Mazuin Zahid, a motoring analyst at Caspian Research. "The luxury car market, especially, is picking up, showing people still have money to splash on cars."

Motor industry executives said demand for heavily-taxed imported cars such as Mercedes Benz, BMW, Volvo and Honda -- and luxury 4WDs such as the Land Rover and Chrysler Jeep -- have grown visibly, although market share was below 10 percent.

The motor traders group said cars made by the local DRB-Hicom group and Perusahaan Otomobil Kedua Sdn Bhd (Perodua) continued to dominate sales, with a joint market share of 83 percent in the first 10 months of 1996.

DRB-Hicom, controlled by Malaysian "car king" Yahaya Ahmad, distributes the Proton range of economic saloon and sporty cars, made by associates Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd and Diversified Resources Bhd
Perodua, a Japanese-Malaysian venture, produces the subcompact Kancil.

Japan's Honda and Toyota remained the best-selling foreign cars. Industry executives attributed their success to competitively-priced new models, such as the 70,000 ringgit ($28,000) Honda City, which had a waiting period of more than a year before delivery.
